```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "",
  class.output = "spax-output",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 100

This guide uses the bundled Cornwall GP data, described in [The Cornwall GP
example data](cornwall-data.html).

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

Floating catchment area (FCA) methods combine demand, facility supply and
travel weights into an accessibility index. They differ in how they weight
travel. This guide computes three of them on the same inputs and compares the
results: the enhanced two-step FCA (E2SFCA) from [Getting started](spax.html),
the original 2SFCA and the modified 2SFCA (M2SFCA). A last section adds two
variants that first share each cell's demand among practices, 3SFCA and
Huff-2SFCA, and a final one lets several demand groups, such as age bands,
have their own decay. For a fitted allocation model with an outside option, see
[Choosing an FCA index or an allocation model](model-choice.html).

## The inputs

The inputs are those of [Getting started](spax.html): the WorldPop 2020
population grid (estimated residents per cell of about 1 km, a count rather
than a density), GP FTE excluding GPs in training, and travel minutes to each
mainland practice. The grid and the workforce come from different sources and
dates (2020 and 2026).

```{r inputs}
# Residents per grid cell, and travel minutes with one layer per practice
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")

# Mainland only: the Isles of Scilly have no road link to the mainland
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- travel[[gp$practice]]

# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice, then drop the
# empty margin the islands leave behind
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel)))
travel <- crop(travel, pop)

# Layers must line up with the practice table and the population grid
stopifnot(
  identical(names(travel), gp$practice),
  compareGeom(pop, travel)
)

c(
  cells = sum(!is.na(values(pop))),
  practices = nrow(gp),
  residents = round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  gp_fte = round(sum(gp$gp_fte_extg), 1)
)
```

[Preparing your own data](data-prep.html) explains these steps in detail.

## Three ways to weight travel

Each method gathers demand to practices with one set of weights, divides each
practice's supply by the demand it gathered, and spreads those ratios back to
cells with a second set of weights.

| Method | Weights when gathering demand | Weights when spreading ratios |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 2SFCA | 1 within 15 minutes, 0 beyond | The same |
| E2SFCA | Gaussian decay, scale 10 minutes | The same |
| M2SFCA | Gaussian decay, scale 10 minutes | The Gaussian weight squared |

The 15-minute threshold and the 10-minute scale are choices for this guide,
not estimates. With the Gaussian scale of 10 minutes, a practice 10 minutes
away keeps about 61% of its weight and one 20 minutes away about 14%.
`demand_normalize = "identity"` uses the weights unchanged when practices
gather demand, as in the original E2SFCA.

```{r methods}
twosfca <- spax_2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  threshold = 15,  # minutes
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

e2sfca <- spax_e2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity",
  id_col = "practice",  # matches supply rows to travel layers
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

m2sfca <- spax_m2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity",
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
```

Each result is a `spax` object whose `accessibility` member is a raster of GP
FTE per resident. The maps show all three in GP FTE per 1,000 residents on one
colour scale.

```{r methods-map, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three raster maps of mainland Cornwall on one colour scale in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: E2SFCA changes smoothly, 2SFCA has sharp steps at the 15-minute catchment edges, and M2SFCA is lower throughout."}
# Stack the three surfaces and draw them on one shared colour scale
all_three <- 1000 * c(
  e2sfca$accessibility,
  twosfca$accessibility,
  m2sfca$accessibility
)
names(all_three) <- c(
  "E2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min",
  "2SFCA, 15 min",
  "M2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min"
)
shared_range <- range(values(all_three), na.rm = TRUE)
plot(
  all_three,
  nc = 3,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = shared_range,
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000")
)
```

## Compare the values

```{r compare}
# Cell values as plain vectors, per 1,000 residents, and residents per cell
per_1000 <- function(x) 1000 * values(x$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
a <- per_1000(e2sfca)
b <- per_1000(twosfca)
m <- per_1000(m2sfca)
p <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)

# Cell quantiles and the index of the average resident
describe <- function(x) {
  c(
    quantile(x, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
    resident_weighted = weighted.mean(x, p, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
round(
  rbind(
    E2SFCA = describe(a),
    `2SFCA` = describe(b),
    M2SFCA = describe(m)
  ),
  2
)

# Total supply per 1,000 residents, for comparison
round(1000 * sum(gp$gp_fte_extg) / sum(p, na.rm = TRUE), 2)

# An index of zero in 2SFCA means no practice within 15 minutes
c(
  residents_beyond_15_min = round(sum(p[b == 0], na.rm = TRUE)),
  correlation_2sfca = round(cor(a, b, use = "complete.obs"), 2),
  correlation_m2sfca = round(cor(a, m, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
)
```

```{r compare-values, include = FALSE}
cor_2sfca <- round(cor(a, b, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
cor_m2sfca <- round(cor(a, m, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
beyond_15 <- format(round(sum(p[b == 0], na.rm = TRUE)), big.mark = ",")
```

The quantiles describe grid cells, and most cells are rural. Weighting by
residents answers a different question: the index the average resident sees.
For E2SFCA and 2SFCA that average equals total GP FTE per 1,000 residents,
because each uses the same weights in both steps and every practice gathers
some demand. These indices redistribute the supply; they do not create or lose
any. M2SFCA does not keep that total: its squared weights are smaller than the
weights used to gather demand, so part of the supply is not spread back to
anyone, and it discounts most strongly the cells whose practices are far away.

The three surfaces broadly agree on where access is higher: E2SFCA correlates
at `r cor_2sfca` with 2SFCA and at `r cor_m2sfca` with M2SFCA across cells.
2SFCA shows sharp steps at the 15-minute edges and a longer upper tail, and
the `r beyond_15` residents with no practice within 15 minutes get an index of
zero. The decay versions change gradually instead. All three depend on
choices, the threshold or the decay scale, that this guide does not estimate
from data. [The E2SFCA calculation step by step](e2sfca-steps.html) rebuilds
the E2SFCA and M2SFCA surfaces from their parts.

The index has supply-per-demand units. It is not a share of people who use a
practice, a waiting time or an observed rate of care.

## Selection weights: 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA

With the weights above, the weights of all practices at one cell need not add
up to 1, so where many practices are close each of them counts the same
residents. Two further variants first share each cell's demand among the
practices. At each cell, the **selection weight** `G` of a practice is its
share of the cell's weights, so the shares at a cell add up to 1. Both steps
then use the kernel `K = W * G` in place of the decay weights `W`: a practice
gathers demand and spreads its ratio back to cells with the same weights.

| Method | Selection weight `G` of a practice at a cell | Weights in both steps |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 3SFCA | Its Gaussian weight, divided by the sum of these weights over the cell's practices | `W * G` |
| Huff-2SFCA | Its Gaussian weight times its GP FTE, divided by the sum of these products over the cell's practices | `W * G` |

Huff-2SFCA puts the attractiveness of a practice into the share. By default the
attractiveness is the supply measure, here GP FTE, raised to the power
`alpha = 1`. Both functions also use the Gaussian decay for the selection
weights, because `selection_params` defaults to `decay_params`; they have no
`demand_normalize` argument, because the shares already divide each cell's
demand. This differs from `demand_normalize = "standard"` in `spax_e2sfca()`,
which divides the weights that gather demand only.

```{r selection-methods}
sfca3 <- spax_3sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

huff <- spax_huff2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"  # also the attractiveness
)
```

3SFCA is the shared FCA calculation with a different kernel, so it can be
rebuilt from `calc_decay()`, `calc_choice()` and `compute_access()`. The check
is silent when the selection weights add up to 1 at every cell and the
building blocks reproduce `spax_3sfca()`.

```{r selection-blocks}
w <- calc_decay(travel, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10)  # decay weights W
g <- calc_choice(w)  # selection weights G: each cell's weights over their sum
k <- w * g           # the kernel of both steps

by_blocks <- compute_access(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  demand_weights = k,
  access_weights = k,
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    range(values(sum(g), mat = FALSE), na.rm = TRUE),
    c(1, 1)
  )),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    values(by_blocks, mat = FALSE),
    values(sfca3$accessibility, mat = FALSE),
    tolerance = 1e-10,
    check.attributes = FALSE
  ))
)
```

Each variant uses one kernel in both steps, as E2SFCA and 2SFCA do, so it
returns the supply of every practice that gathers demand, here all of them:
residents times index, summed over cells, equals the total GP FTE. The check
shows that sum as a share of total GP FTE. M2SFCA squares the access-side
weights and returns only part of it.

```{r selection-supply}
# Residents times index, summed over cells, as a share of total GP FTE
returned <- function(x) {
  sum(p * values(x$accessibility, mat = FALSE), na.rm = TRUE) /
    sum(gp$gp_fte_extg)
}
round(
  c(
    E2SFCA = returned(e2sfca),
    `2SFCA` = returned(twosfca),
    M2SFCA = returned(m2sfca),
    `3SFCA` = returned(sfca3),
    `Huff-2SFCA` = returned(huff)
  ),
  6
)
```

The maps put E2SFCA, 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA on the colour scale of the first map,
in GP FTE per 1,000 residents.

```{r selection-map, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three raster maps of mainland Cornwall on the colour scale of the first map, in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: E2SFCA changes smoothly and is low on Bodmin Moor and at the tips of the peninsulas, while 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA are patchier, stay low on Bodmin Moor and are higher than E2SFCA at the tips of the peninsulas, most clearly at the Lizard."}
# Same colour scale as the first map; the new surfaces lie within its range
selection_maps <- 1000 * c(
  e2sfca$accessibility,
  sfca3$accessibility,
  huff$accessibility
)
names(selection_maps) <- c(
  "E2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min",
  "3SFCA, Gaussian 10 min",
  "Huff-2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min"
)
stopifnot(
  min(values(selection_maps), na.rm = TRUE) >= shared_range[1],
  max(values(selection_maps), na.rm = TRUE) <= shared_range[2]
)
plot(
  selection_maps,
  nc = 3,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = shared_range,
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000")
)
```

```{r selection-compare}
a3 <- per_1000(sfca3)
ah <- per_1000(huff)

# Cell quantiles and the resident-weighted index, as for the other methods
round(
  rbind(
    E2SFCA = describe(a),
    `3SFCA` = describe(a3),
    `Huff-2SFCA` = describe(ah)
  ),
  2
)

# Agreement across cells
c(
  correlation_e2sfca_3sfca = round(cor(a, a3, use = "complete.obs"), 2),
  correlation_e2sfca_huff = round(cor(a, ah, use = "complete.obs"), 2),
  correlation_3sfca_huff = round(cor(a3, ah, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
)
```

```{r selection-values, include = FALSE}
cor_e2sfca_3sfca <- round(cor(a, a3, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
cor_3sfca_huff <- round(cor(a3, ah, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
```

The resident-weighted index is the same for the three, because each returns
the total supply. They differ in which cells the supply is credited to: across
cells E2SFCA correlates at `r cor_e2sfca_3sfca` with 3SFCA, while adding
attractiveness to 3SFCA changes the surface less (a correlation of
`r cor_3sfca_huff`). On the maps, 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA are higher than E2SFCA
at the ends of the Lizard and Land's End peninsulas, where E2SFCA is lowest,
and they are lowest on Bodmin Moor, where E2SFCA is also low. With `alpha = 0` attractiveness has no
effect and Huff-2SFCA equals 3SFCA.

```{r selection-alpha}
no_attractiveness <- spax_huff2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  alpha = 0,
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  values(no_attractiveness$accessibility, mat = FALSE),
  values(sfca3$accessibility, mat = FALSE),
  tolerance = 1e-10,
  check.attributes = FALSE
)))
```

As for the other methods, the index has supply-per-demand units, and the decay
scale, the attractiveness measure and `alpha` are choices that this guide does
not estimate from data. `?spax_3sfca` and `?spax_huff2sfca` describe
`selection_params`, which gives the selection weights another decay or a
catchment limit, and cite the methods.

## Several demand groups

Residents can differ in how far they travel, for example by age or by the
transport they have. Give `demand` as a named list of single-layer rasters, one
per group, and each group gets its own surface. The Cornwall data have no
age split, so this section builds one for illustration. It is not data: it
assumes that the share of residents in an older group rises in a straight line
from 15% at the western edge of the grid to 35% at the eastern edge, and that
the older group travels less far to a practice, with a Gaussian scale of 8
minutes against 12 for the younger group. All of these numbers are
illustrative choices.

```{r groups}
# An illustrative older share that rises from west to east, not data
older_share <- mask(init(pop, "x"), pop)
rng <- unlist(global(older_share, range, na.rm = TRUE))
older_share <- 0.15 + 0.20 * (older_share - rng[1]) / (rng[2] - rng[1])

groups <- list(
  younger = pop * (1 - older_share),
  older = pop * older_share
)

# One decay per group, named by the group IDs
by_group <- spax_e2sfca(
  demand = groups,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel,
  decay_params = list(
    younger = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 12),
    older = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 8)
  ),
  demand_normalize = "identity",
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
names(by_group$accessibility)
```

All groups compete for the same GP time: step 1 adds up the demand of the
groups that reaches each practice, each with its own weights, so a practice has
one demand total and one supply-to-demand ratio. Step 2 then gives each group
its own surface from those shared ratios, using its own weights. The layer
ending in `.all` is the overall surface, the average of the group surfaces
weighted by the demand of each cell. A group whose travel reaches no practice
from a cell counts with an index of 0 there, so the overall layer shows it as
no access.

```{r groups-map, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three raster maps of mainland Cornwall on one colour scale in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: the younger group, the older group with a shorter travel scale, which is lower everywhere, and the overall surface between the two."}
group_maps <- 1000 * by_group$accessibility
names(group_maps) <- c(
  "Younger, Gaussian 12 min",
  "Older, Gaussian 8 min",
  "Overall, demand-weighted"
)
plot(
  group_maps,
  nc = 3,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = range(values(group_maps), na.rm = TRUE),
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000")
)
```

```{r groups-compare}
# Demand-weighted mean index per 1,000 residents of each group, and overall
mean_index <- function(layer, weight) {
  x <- 1000 * values(by_group$accessibility[[layer]], mat = FALSE)
  w <- values(weight, mat = FALSE)
  weighted.mean(x, w, na.rm = TRUE)
}
round(
  c(
    younger = mean_index("gp_fte_extg.younger", groups$younger),
    older = mean_index("gp_fte_extg.older", groups$older),
    overall = mean_index("gp_fte_extg.all", pop)
  ),
  2
)
```

```{r groups-values, include = FALSE}
mean_young <- round(mean_index("gp_fte_extg.younger", groups$younger), 2)
mean_old <- round(mean_index("gp_fte_extg.older", groups$older), 2)
```

The average younger resident sees `r mean_young` GP FTE per 1,000 residents
and the average older resident `r mean_old`; the overall value lies between
them, nearer the younger group because that group is the larger one in every
cell. With a shorter scale, every practice at a positive travel time gets a smaller
weight for the older group, so its index is lower. The gap reflects the assumed travel scales and the
assumed split, not any observed difference between age groups.

Transport modes are another use. Give `distance` as a named list with one
travel stack per group, for example one for car and one for public transport;
the stacks must name the same practices in the same order, and
`decay_params` can be given per group in the same way. This follows the
structure of the multi-modal 2SFCA of [Tao et al.
(2018)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3132-8) (their equations 3-5), in
which the modes share the supply and the travel times differ by mode, and
generalizes it to a decay that differs by group. Earlier multi-modal 2SFCA
work includes [Mao and Nekorchuk
(2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.healthplace.2013.08.008) and [Langford,
Higgs and Fry (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.healthplace.2015.11.007).
`?spax_e2sfca` lists which arguments can be given per group.
